# 1982 Los Angeles Rams–Green Bay Packers game

The **1982 Los Angeles Rams–Green Bay Packers game** was a National Football League (NFL) regular season contest played on **September 12, 1982**, at Milwaukee County Stadium in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. It was the season opener for both teams in the strike-shortened 1982 NFL season . The game is notable for the **Packers' historic 23-point comeback**, overcoming a 23-0 halftime deficit to win 35-23, which was the largest comeback in Packers history at that time .

## Game background

The 1982 NFL season was significantly impacted by a **57-day players' strike** that reduced the regular season from 16 games to just nine games per team . This game marked the opening week of this abbreviated season, with both teams beginning with a 0-0 record . The Rams were coached by Ray Malavasi, while the Packers were led by Bart Starr in his second season as head coach .

The game was played at Milwaukee County Stadium, which served as the Packers' secondary home venue from 1953 to 1994 . The official attendance was 53,694 .

## Game summary

### First half

The first half was dominated entirely by the **Los Angeles Rams**, who capitalized on three Packers turnovers to build a commanding 23-0 lead by halftime .

In the first quarter, the Rams struck quickly when Gerry Ellis fumbled on a short run, and the Rams recovered and returned the ball to midfield. A 22-yard pass from quarterback Bert Jones to Wendell Tyler set up a short rushing touchdown by Tyler, giving the Rams an early 7-0 lead . After another Packers fumble by quarterback Lynn Dickey, the Rams added a 32-yard field goal by Mike Lansford to extend their lead to 10-0 .

The second quarter saw the Rams continue their dominance. A 43-yard pass from Jones to Willie Miller put the Rams in scoring position, and Jones subsequently completed an 8-yard touchdown pass to Mike Barber, making the score 17-0 . The Rams added two more field goals before halftime - a 29-yarder and a 28-yarder by Lansford - to take a commanding 23-0 lead into the locker room .

The Packers managed only **66 net yards** in the first half and committed four turnovers (two fumbles and two interceptions) .

### Second half

The second half saw a **complete reversal of fortunes** as the Packers scored 35 unanswered points to pull off one of the most dramatic comebacks in NFL history .

The Packers got on the scoreboard in the third quarter with a 4-yard touchdown pass from Dickey to tight end Paul Coffman. The drive was set up by a defensive pass interference penalty that gave the Packers 28 yards . The Packers struck again shortly thereafter, with Eddie Lee Ivery scoring on a 3-yard run. The key play of this drive was a 42-yard pass from Dickey to Coffman . By the end of the third quarter, the Packers had cut the Rams' lead to 23-14 .

The fourth quarter saw the Packers complete their comeback. After the Rams failed on a long field goal attempt, the Packers took over and drove 66 yards in five plays, with Dickey throwing a 15-yard touchdown pass to James Lofton to make the score 23-21 .

The turning point came on the ensuing kickoff when Rams returner Robert Alexander fumbled, and the Packers recovered at the Los Angeles 10-yard line. Dickey needed only one play to find Coffman in the end zone for a 10-yard touchdown pass, giving the Packers their first lead of the game at 28-23 .

The Packers sealed the victory with a 27-yard touchdown run by Ivery with about three minutes remaining in the game . The Packers defense also contributed to the comeback by holding the Rams to just four first downs in the second half and intercepting the Rams twice while forcing a fumble .

**Los Angeles Rams (0-1)**

* **Passing**: Bert Jones 17/31, 202 yards, 1 TD, 2 INT

* **Rushing**: Wendell Tyler 14 carries, 57 yards, 1 TD

* **Receiving**: Willie Miller 3 receptions, 78 yards; Mike Guman 4 receptions, 37 yards

**Green Bay Packers (1-0)**

* **Passing**: Lynn Dickey 17/27, 237 yards, 3 TD, 3 INT

* **Rushing**: Eddie Lee Ivery 17 carries, 109 yards, 2 TD

* **Receiving**: John Jefferson 6 receptions, 116 yards; Paul Coffman 4 receptions, 66 yards, 2 TD; James Lofton 4 receptions, 59 yards, 1 TD

## Aftermath and significance

The Packers' 23-point comeback was the **largest in franchise history** at that time . It remained the Packers' record until December 15, 2013, when they matched it in a game against the Dallas Cowboys . The comeback is widely regarded as one of the most dramatic in NFL history .

For the Rams, the loss was particularly devastating as it came in their season opener and set a negative tone for their campaign. The Rams would go on to finish the strike-shortened 1982 season with a 2-7 record .

The Packers, meanwhile, used the momentum from this victory to finish the abbreviated season with a 5-3-1 record . The game is still remembered as one of the most remarkable comebacks in Packers history and a highlight of the 1982 season .

The 1982 season was unique due to the players' strike, and this game stands out as one of its most memorable moments . It demonstrated the unpredictable nature of professional football and showcased the Packers' resilience under coach Bart Starr .

#### Your Privacy Choices

In order to provide you with free high-quality content that you love to watch and offers that are more relevant to you, the National Football League collects and shares certain personal information. Because we respect your privacy, we also provide you choices with respect to your personal information. You may use the toggles in the sections below to opt out of certain cookies (e.g., pixels), including the use of targeting cookies that may be deemed to result in the “sale” or “sharing” of personal information under certain United States laws. If you choose to opt out of these cookies, you will still see ads, though they may be less relevant to you. You are always free to turn optional cookies back on using this cookie preference center. For more information about how we collect and share your personal information and other privacy choices you may have, refer to our 

[Privacy Policy.](https://www.packers.com/fans/privacy-policy)

#### Strictly Necessary

These cookies are necessary for the website to function and cannot be switched off in our systems. They are usually only set in response to actions made by you which amount to a request for services, such as setting your privacy preferences, logging in or filling in forms. You can set your browser to block or alert you about these cookies, but some parts of the site might not work as a result.

#### Performance

- [x] Performance 

These cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance of our site. They help us to know which pages are the most and least popular and see how visitors move around the site. If you do not allow these cookies we will not know when you have visited our site, and will not be able to monitor its performance.

#### Functional

- [x] Functional 

These cookies enable the website to provide enhanced functionality and personalization. They may be set by us or by third party providers whose services we have added to our pages. If you do not allow these cookies then some or all of these services may not function properly.

#### Selling, Sharing, Targeted Advertising

- [x] Selling, Sharing, Targeted Advertising 

Under certain state laws in the United States, “sale” or “sharing” of personal information is defined broadly and in a way that may include allowing third parties to receive certain information for certain functions, including but not limited to targeted advertising. These laws may provide residents with the right to opt out of such sales or sharing of their personal information. To opt out of the sale or sharing of your personal information collected through cookies, move the toggle to the left and select "Confirm My Choices". If you choose to opt out of this data sharing, you will still see ads, though they may be less relevant to you. These ads may be based on historical information or information shared or sold by other sources. You will need to renew this choice each time you clear your cookies or use a new browser or device. This opt-out applies only to certain cookie (“online”) data we have about you. If you wish to communicate your opt out choices with respect to selling or sharing other types of data beyond cookies (e.g., “offline” data) you may do so by submitting a privacy request form via the “Your Privacy Choices” link located in the footer of this website’s homepage.

![Image 3: 041005dickey_a.jpg](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/f_auto/packers/nbh0l1iq25edeabhos99.jpg)

_GREATEST COMEBACK IN PACKERS HISTORY, KEY WESTERN CONFERENCE PLAYOFF HIGHLIGHT 7-DECADE SERIES WITH RAMS_

The Packers and the [St. Louis Rams](http://www.stlouisrams.com/), who will make mutual history next week when they meet on the "Monday Night Football" showcase for the first time, have forged more than a few historic adventures over the course of their seven-decade "association."

Curiously, two of the most memorable occurred in Milwaukee - at County Stadium, the Packers' second home from 1953-1994, which since has fallen to the wrecking ball.

Chief among them, without question, was a critical 28-7 victory over the Rams in a 1967 Western Conference playoff which propelled the Packers into the fabled "Ice Bowl" against the [Dallas Cowboys](http://www.dallascowboys.com/), played in Lambeau Field just eight days later.

Close behind, from the historical perspective, was a salutary happening on Sept. 12, 1982.

The Green and Gold, down 23-0 at halftime, proceeded to execute the most dramatic comeback in team annals, erupting for 35 consecutive unanswered points in the second half to depart County Stadium with a 35-23 victory.

From the overall standpoint, the Packers dominated the early years of the series, launched in 1937 when the Rams were based in Cleveland, winning 12 and tying one of the first 14 games (they also have won five of the last seven meetings). But the Rams caught up during the '50s and today lead the series, having won 44 games to the Packers' 39.

There also have been two ties - the most recent a 24-24 standoff at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum in 1964 (the Rams became the NFL's first West Coast team when they moved to Los Angeles in 1946).

In addition, there recently has been a second playoff game, a divisional showdown in which the Rams posted a 45-17 victory at St. Louis on Jan. 20, 2002 (The Rams had moved to St. Louis in 1995).

The '67 playoff contest matched the Packers, champions of the NFL's Central Division (9-4-1) and the Rams, the Coastal Division champions (11-1-2), to determine the winner of the Western Conference title. The survivors would advance to the NFL Championship Game against Dallas in what became the "Ice Bowl."

On that occasion, things were more than somewhat chancy for the Packers in the early going, which saw the Rams move out to a 7-0 first quarter lead by way of a 29-yard Roman Gabriel scoring pass to Bernie Casey.

To compound the problem, the Rams again threatened to score early in the second quarter when defensive back Chuck Lamson waylaid a Bart Starr pass and returned it to Green Bay's 10-yard-line.

Fortuitously, premier pass rusher Henry Jordan sacked Gabriel for a 7-yard loss on third down, forcing Los Angeles to attempt a field goal by Bruce Gossett, an effort which was blocked by linebacker Dave Robinson.

One exchange later, rookie running back Travis Williams, who had become a sensation at mid-season, broke into the open over the right side and streaked 46 yards to the end zone, Don Chandler adding the extra point to tie the score at 7.

The Rams also came up empty on their next possession, Gossett's 46-yard field goal attempt falling short, and the Packers' Willie Wood staked the Green and Gold to prime field position, returning the failed kick 44 yards to the Green Bay 45.

From there, Starr had the Packers in the end zone in 7 plays, firing a 17-yard, third-down strike to wide receiver Carroll Dale for the score. Chandler's conversion made it 14-7 at the intermission.

Taking over the game in the second half, the Packers scored on a 4-yard run by running back Chuck Mercein in the third quarter and a 2-yard run by Williams in the fourth quarter while a tightfisted defense continued to hold the Rams scoreless the rest of the way.

One of the most significant victories in team annals, it set the stage for the Packers to make NFL history by becoming the only team to win three consecutive league championships since the advent of the playoff system in 1933 by defeating the Cowboys for the '67 title in the "Ice Bowl," 21-17.

Behind the scenes, the scheduling of the back-to-back post-season contests spoke volumes about Lombardi's confidence in himself and his football team. As the Packers' general manager, he had assigned the first playoff to Milwaukee, sure in his own mind that the Green and Gold would be in the NFL Championship Game - in Green Bay - eight days later.

The subsequent "comeback classic" in '82 was much like two very different games, with the Rams converting three first half turnovers into 13 points en route to that 23-0 intermission lead.

Overall, two lost fumbles and two Rams interceptions contributed substantially to the Packers' scoreless state at halftime, a point at which they had a modest 66 net yards to show for their efforts.

But things were dramatically different in the second half. Quarterback Lynn Dickey began to hit his receivers with admirable frequency and the defense collaborated by restricting the Rams to "three-and-out" on their first two third-quarter possessions.

After the first such defensive intervention, Dickey guided the Packers 55 yards to their first touchdown of the afternoon, hitting tight end Paul Coffman with a 4-yard strike for the score.

The Green and Gold were even more expeditious on the second possession of the period, winging 47 yards in three plays for the touchdown, set up by Dickey's 42-yard "bomb" to Coffman, which positioned the Packers at the 3-yard line. From there, halfback Eddie Lee Ivery burst into the end zone over right tackle on the next play. And. after Jan Stenerud's second conversion, it was a more reassuring 23-14, but still a long way to go.

A series of four "three-and-outs," two by each team, and a third Dickey interception subsequently intervened before the Packers engineered a decisive breakthrough early in the fourth quarter.

Taking over at their own 34 after Rams placekicker Mike Lansford 's 51-yard field goal attempt veered wide left, Dickey had the home forces in the end zone in four plays, the score coming on a 15-yard pass to wide receiver James Lofton. Stenerud's conversion pared the Rams' lead to two points, 23-21.

Then, right on the heels of that highly favorable development, Rams returner Kermit Alexander fumbled the succeeding kickoff and the Packers' Guy Prather recovered at the Los Angeles 10-yard line.

Dickey needed only one play from there, finding Coffman in the heart of the end zone for the score and sending the Packers into the lead for the first time at the 3:48 mark of the final period.

The suddenly embattled Rams responded with a pair of first downs following the next kickoff but an 8-yard Mike Butler sack of L.A. quarterback Bert Jones stalled the drive.

One exchange later, Packers linebacker George Cumby intercepted a Jones pass and the Packers promptly set about the finishing touches.

Ivery opened the 66-yard drive modestly enough with a 2-yard gain, after which Dickey hit Coffman with a 10-yard pass and running back Mike Meade broke through the middle for a 19-yard advance, "improved" by a 5-yard face mask penalty on the Rams.

Meade next hit left tackle for 3 yards, setting the stage for Ivery to bolt up the middle on a 27-yard draw for the game's final touchdown with 3:06 remaining in the game.

Stenerud then added the Packers' 35th consecutive, unanswered point with his fifth conversion, completing the most remarkable comeback in team annals.

_Continuing an association with the team that is more than 55 years old, Lee Remmel was [named the first official Team Historian](https://www.packers.com/news-and-events/article-1/packers-name-lee-remmel-team-historian/9eb331e1-5aa4-11df-a3b6-528cc843f916) of the Green Bay Packers in February 2004. The former *Green Bay Press-Gazette_ reporter and Packers public relations director, Remmel will write regular columns for Packers.com as part of his new assignment.

In addition to those articles, Remmel will answer fan questions in a monthly Q&A column. To submit a question to Remmel, [click here](https://www.packers.com/fans/ask/lee_remmel/). *

5.title: Flashback 1982: The Green Bay Packers Overcome a 23-Point Deficit and Comeback to Beat the Los Angeles Rams 35-23
5.description: Featured Flashback 1983: The Green Bay Packers overcame a 23-0 halftime deficit and completed a record-setting comeback to win 35-23.
5.content:
Things didn’t look good for the [Green Bay Packers](https://thepackerspost.com/) in their 1982 season opener against the Los Angeles Rams at Milwaukee County Stadium. They trailed 23-0 at the half and looked lethargic. But the Packers managed to complete a record-setting comeback to win the game 35-23.

### The Packers Comeback: A Sloppy First Half

As the teams left the field at the half, boos echoed at the stadium. Starting quarterback [Lynn Dickey](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=Lynn+Dickey) threw two interceptions and lost two fumbles in the first half and the Packers had five total turnovers before the break. Running back [Gerry Ellis](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=Gerry+Ellis) left the game with a knee injury which further hurt the Pack. [Bart Starr](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=Bart+Starr)’s team just looked flat.

But when the teams came out for the second half, the Packers turned it all around. They scored 35 unanswered points to beat the Rams 35-23.

In the first half, the Rams took advantage of the Packers turnovers to take control of the game. Wendell Tyler opened the scoring with a four-yard touchdown run in the first quarter. Bert Jones threw an eight-yard touchdown pass to tight end Mike Barber in the second quarter and barefooted kicker Mike Lansford booted three field goals to give the Rams a 23-0 lead.

### The Packers Comeback: Decisions for Bart Starr

Starr said he never considered replacing the struggling Dickey at halftime. “It’s easy to think in terms of ‘maybe you should make a change’”, Starr said. “But I’ve seen too many good quarterbacks go even three quarters and not be having a very good day and all of a sudden they find it.”

### The Packers Comeback: A Record Setting Rally

In the second half, Dickey found it and he looked like a different player. The Packers came alive on both sides of the ball. The Packers got on the board with a four-yard touchdown pass from Dickey to tight end [Paul Coffman](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=Paul+Coffman) and the lead was cut to 23-7.

Green Bay’s defense stepped up and didn’t allow the Rams a first down for the entire third quarter and gave up only four first downs in the second half. The defense sacked Jones four times with [Mike Douglass](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=Mike+Douglass), [Ezra Johnson](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=Ezra+Johnson), [Terry Jones](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=Terry+Jones), and [Casey Merrill](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=Casey+Merrill) each trapping Jones behind the line of scrimmage.

Later in the third quarter, running back [Eddie Lee Ivery](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=Eddie+Lee+Ivery) scored on a three-yard touchdown run and the Packers pulled to within 23-14.

### Completing the Packers Comeback

The Packers had the momentum and they kept it up in the fourth quarter. Dickey found future Hall of Famer [James Lofton](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=James+Lofton) for a 15-yard touchdown pass and the Packers were within two points at 23-21. The score was set up by a 50-yard bomb from Dickey to [John Jefferson](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=John+Jefferson).

On the ensuing kickoff, reserve linebacker [Guy Prather](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=Guy+Prather) hit kick returner Robert Alexander to force a fumble. Prather also fell on the loose ball and the Packers had the ball at the Rams 10. Dickey quickly took advantage and found Coffman on a 10-yard pass to give Green Bay a 28-23 lead.

The Rams tried to respond and started a drive but linebacker [George Cumby](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=George+Cumby) intercepted Jones at the Green Bay 30 to end that threat. The Packers converted on the turnover as Ivery ran the ball 27 yards for a touchdown to make it 35-23.

Linebacker [John Anderson](https://thepackerspost.com/?s=John+Anderson) clinched the win when he picked off Jones in the fourth quarter to end the Rams last threat. It was the third turnover the Packers forced in the fourth quarter.

### The Start of Bart Starr’s Best Coaching Season

Ivery had a strong game, running for 109 yards and two touchdowns and catching two passes for 32 yards. Jefferson led all Packers receivers with six catches for 116 yards while Coffman had two touchdown catches.

Jones, who was making his first start for the Rams after being acquired in a trade from the Baltimore Colts was blunt in his postgame comments. “Damn, we should have won that game,” he told reporters. “It’s tough to lose anytime, but this way certainly sticks a finger in the sore.”

After the game, Starr called the performance, “The greatest comeback I’ve ever witnessed. I’m at a loss for words to tell you how proud I am of this football team,” as his team got off to a 1-0 start. The Packers would beat the Giants on Monday Night Football the following week to get off to a 2-0 start before a players’ strike disrupted the season. Green Bay finished the year 5-3-1 and made the playoffs for the first time in a decade.

The 23-point comeback is still tied for the Packers biggest comeback of all time. It was a magic moment for the Packers and for Starr who enjoyed his most successful season as Packers coach in 1982.

NFL's Biggest Comebacks by Franchise
====================================

#### [SI Staff](https://www.si.com/author/si-staff) | Nov 25, 2013

![Image 22: NFL's Biggest Comebacks by Franchise](https://www.si.com/.image/c_fill,w_720,ar_16:9,f_auto,q_auto,g_auto/MTY4MjU5NDY1OTE2Nzg2NTg5/new-england-patriots.jpg)

NFL's Biggest Comebacks by Franchise / 

[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=531030426978426&display=popup&href=https:%2F%2Fwww.si.com%2Fnfl%2F2013%2F11%2F25%2Fnfl-biggest-comebacks-franchise)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=NFL%27s%20Biggest%20Comebacks%20by%20Franchise&url=https:%2F%2Fwww.si.com%2Fnfl%2F2013%2F11%2F25%2Fnfl-biggest-comebacks-franchise)[](http://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https:%2F%2Fwww.si.com%2Fnfl%2F2013%2F11%2F25%2Fnfl-biggest-comebacks-franchise&title=NFL%27s%20Biggest%20Comebacks%20by%20Franchise)

* * *

NFL's Biggest Comebacks by Franchise
------------------------------------

### New England Patriots

![Image 23: New England Patriots](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY1OTE2Nzg2NTg5/new-england-patriots.jpg)

Stephan Savoia/AP

SI.com presents the biggest comeback by franchise in the [Super Bowl](https://www.si.com/super-bowl) era, beginning with New England, which was down 24-0 at the half against visiting Denver. But [Tom Brady](https://www.si.com/nfl/player/tom-brady) threw three touchdown passes into the teeth of a 22-mph wind in the second half as the Patriots scored 31 points in a row. Peyton Manning's touchdown pass late in the fourth quarter forced overtime, where the Broncos' Tony Carter ran into Ryan Allen's punt after it bounced, Nate Ebner recovered for the Patriots at the Broncos 13-yard line and Stephen Gostkowski kicked a 31-yard field goal with 1:56 left in OT to give New England a 34-31 win.

### Buffalo Bills

![Image 24: Buffalo Bills](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY2MTg0NTAxMTQ5/buffalo-bills.jpg)

John Biever/SI

The Bills trailed the Oilers 35-3 just after halftime in the Wild Card game now known as "The Comeback." It looked like Buffalo's quest for a third straight Super Bowl appearance would end in the first round. But Frank Reich threw four second-half touchdowns, including three to Andre Reed, and the Bills won 41-38 in overtime. Buffalo's victory remains the largest comeback in NFL history.

### Carolina Panthers

![Image 25: Carolina Panthers](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY1OTE2NzIxMDUz/carolina-panthers.jpg)

Brad Mangin/SI

The Panthers were coming off a Super Bowl appearance but had started the season 1-7. They fell behind the 49ers by 17, but Jake Delhomme led the comeback by throwing for 303 yards and three touchdowns. The win helped jumpstart the Panthers to a 6-2 finish. It also matched the team's comeback in the 2003 season opener, when three Delhomme touchdowns led it past Jacksonville.

### Chicago Bears

![Image 26: Chicago Bears](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY2MTg2MDc0MDEz/chicago-bears.jpg)

Paul Connors, Roy Dabner/AP

Cardinals coach Dennis Green's rant -- "They are who we thought they were." -- is the most famous part of Chicago's comeback from 20 points down in the third quarter. But the most impressive part of the win might be that the team didn't score an offensive touchdown. Quarterback Rex Grossman committed six turnovers and Chicago's three touchdowns came on two fumble returns and a punt return. The Bears also overcame a 20-point deficit against Tampa Bay in 1987.

### Cincinnati Bengals | Dec. 24, 1995

![Image 27: Cincinnati Bengals](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY2MTg0NTY2Njg1/cincinnati-bengals.jpg)

Scott Halleran/Getty Images

The Vikings learned during the game that they had been eliminated from playoff contention. The Bengals took advantage of Minnesota's letdown to overcome a 24-3 halftime deficit. Cincinnati scored 24 unanswered points in the second half. The comeback tied a franchise record set against Seattle in 1981.

### Denver Broncos

![Image 28: Denver Broncos](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY1OTE3NjM4NTU3/denver-broncos.jpg)

Jeff Gross/Getty Images

The Broncos had a 2-3 record to start Peyton Manning's first season with the team. The Chargers jumped out to a 24-0 lead at halftime, and Denver's playoff hopes looked like they were about to take another hit. But Manning tossed three second-half touchdowns and Denver's defense scored twice en route to a 35-24 win. It was the first of 11 straight wins by the Broncos to end the regular season. Denver also had overcome a 24-point deficit in 1979 against the Seahawks.

### Detroit Lions

![Image 29: Detroit Lions](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY2MTg4MTA1NjI5/detroit-lions.jpg)

David E. Klutho/SI

A week earlier, the Lions had overcome a 20-point deficit for an overtime win. This time, Detroit dug an even deeper hole. Dallas led 27-3 early in the third quarter, but Detroit's Bobby Carpenter and Chris Houston each returned interceptions for touchdowns. Then, Calvin Johnson dominated the final period with two touchdown catches.

### Green Bay Packers

![Image 30: Green Bay Packers](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY2MTg1NDg0MTg5/green-bay-packers.jpg)

Ronald C. Modra/Sports Imagery/Getty Images

The Rams started the strike-shortened 1982 season with 23 first-half points. The Packers answered with 35 straight points in the second half. Eddie Lee Ivery (pictured) and Paul Coffman scored two touchdowns each, and Green Bay went on to a 5-3-1 record in the nine-game season.

### Miami Dolphins | Dec. 15, 1974

![Image 31: Miami Dolphins](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY2MTg1MzUzMTE3/miami-dolphins.jpg)

Courtesy of fanbase.com

The Dolphins' final regular season tune up started poorly. Early in the second quarter, New England led 24-0. But the Dolphins, winners of back-to-back Super Bowls, rebounded with a 24-0 run of their own. Melvin Baker caught two touchdowns on the way to a 34-27 Miami win. The Dolphins' title defense would end the next week in the first round of the playoffs.

### New Orleans Saints

![Image 32: New Orleans Saints](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY1OTE4MjI4Mzgx/new-orleans-saints.jpg)

Bob Rosato/SI

The Saints won this season's Super Bowl behind its high-powered offense, but its defense helped key its come-from-behind win. After Miami built a 24-3 lead, Darren Sharper and Tracy Porter each returned interceptions for touchdowns in a 46-34 win. The Saints had also overcome 21-point deficits in 1987 and 1969.

### New York Giants

![Image 33: New York Giants](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY1OTE3OTAwNzAx/new-york-giants.jpg)

Neil Leifer/SI

In a game of runs, Washington scored 27 straight points to take a 33-14 lead. But Ron Johnson ran for two touchdowns and Fran Tarkenton hit Tucker Frederickson for a 57-yard score as New York won 35-33. It was the franchise's biggest comeback in the Super Bowl Era.

### Pittsburgh Steelers

![Image 34: Pittsburgh Steelers](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY2MTg4NDk4ODQ1/pittsburgh-steelers.jpg)

Bob Rosato/SI

Kordell Stewart had a breakthrough game a week earlier when he ran for 117 yards and showed off an improved throwing motion. His strong play continued against the Ravens when he ran for two touchdowns and threw for three others as the Steelers overcame a 21-0 deficit.

### San Francisco 49ers

![Image 35: San Francisco 49ers](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY1OTE2MzkzMzcz/san-francisco-49ers.jpg)

Robert Riger/Getty Images

The 49ers were struggling in Bill Walsh's second season in charge and entered with a 5-8 record. The Saints, behind three Archie Manning touchdown passes, took a 35-7 lead into halftime. But Joe Montana, a part-time starter in his second year in the league, threw two touchdowns and ran for another to complete the biggest regular-season comeback in NFL history.

### Seattle Seahawks

![Image 36: Seattle Seahawks](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY2MTg3MzE5MTk3/seattle-seahawks.jpg)

Steve Dykes/Getty Images

Seattle erased a 21-0 deficit in a Week 9, 2013, game against Tampa Bay. Russell Wilson threw a 10-yard touchdown pass to Doug Baldwin with 1:51 left in regulation to tie the game at 24-24 and Steven Hauschka kicked the game-winning 27-yard field goal with 8:11 left in overtime.

### Tampa Bay Buccaneers

![Image 37: Tampa Bay Buccaneers](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY2MTg1OTQyOTQx/tampa-bay-buccaneers.jpg)

John Sleezer/Kansas City Star/MCT via Getty Images

The Buccaneers sent the game to overtime after Jeff Garcia threw a touchdown and completed a two-point conversion. But Tampa Bay may not have won without a fortuitous penalty. Bucs kicker Matt Bryant missed a field goal, but a false start on lineman Jeremy Trueblood gave Tampa Bay another chance. Garcia completed a pass, and Bryant drilled the shorter second attempt.

### Tennessee Titans

![Image 38: Tennessee Titans](https://www.si.com/.image/t_share/MTY4MjU5NDY1OTE4NDkwNTI1/tennessee-titans.jpg)

AP

Earl Campbell ran 38 times for 154 yards and a touchdown as the Houston Oilers overcame Cincinnati's 24-0 advantage. The Oilers went on to reach the AFC Championship Game that season.

Kirk Cousins Put On a Masterclass Explaining How to Play QB in the NFL
======================================================================

The Falcons signal caller got on his soap box.

#### By [Mike Kadlick](https://www.si.com/author/michael-kadlick) | Dec 18, 2025

![Image 43: Kirk Cousins led the Falcons on a game-winning drive last Thursday night.](https://images2.minutemediacdn.com/image/upload/c_crop,w_1198,h_673,x_0,y_0/c_fill,w_720,ar_16:9,f_auto,q_auto,g_auto/images/voltaxMediaLibrary/mmsport/si/01kcs506nyxg67hnw02r.png)

Kirk Cousins led the Falcons on a game-winning drive last Thursday night. / @AtlantaFalcons

* * *

The topic of quarterback development in the NFL has come to the forefront this week following the latest [benching of a former first-round pick in Tua Tagovailoa](https://www.si.com/nfl/dolphins-benching-tua-tagovailoa-for-rookie-quinn-ewers). More specifically, the difference between coverage and pure-progression reads.

In its simplest terms, there are essentially two ways a signal-caller can attack an opposing defense. The first is a pre-snap dissection of coverage—accomplished mainly by identifying where the safeties are aligned—and the other is what’s called a pure progression read, which involves working through your options post-snap, based on the route concept, to find an open receiver._(Note: Pure progression reads are still loosely informed by coverage, though they aren't necessarily dictated by it.)_

Teams across the league use both concepts—some more than others, and vice versa—and lately, a debate over which approach is better for the quarterback has surfaced. Kirk Cousins, now 37 years old and amid his 14th NFL season, has done both throughout his career, and recently delivered a masterclass on the pros and cons of each from the QB's perspective.

Take a look at two-plus minute rant on the matter here:

1982 Los Angeles Rams vs Green Bay Packers
------------------------------------------

| [Los Angeles Rams](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams "1982 Los Angeles Rams") (0–0) | [Green Bay Packers](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Green_Bay_Packers "1982 Green Bay Packers") (0–0) |
| --- | --- |
| 23 | 35 |
| Head coach: [Ray Malavasi](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Ray_Malavasi "Ray Malavasi") | Head coach: [Bart Starr](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Bart_Starr "Bart Starr") |
Date September 12, 1982
Stadium[Milwaukee County Stadium](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Milwaukee_County_Stadium "Milwaukee County Stadium"), Milwaukee, Wisconsin
Attendance 53,694

The [Los Angeles Rams](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Los_Angeles_Rams "Los Angeles Rams") played the [Green Bay Packers](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") in the first game for each team of the [1982 NFL season](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_NFL_season "1982 NFL season") on September 12, 1982, at [Milwaukee County Stadium](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Milwaukee_County_Stadium "Milwaukee County Stadium") in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The recent history of each team differed greatly: the Rams had missed the playoffs in 1981 for the first time in eight seasons, while the Packers had not been to the playoffs since 1972 and had not won a playoff game since 1967. The Rams began the game strong, scoring 23 points in the first half, while shutting the Packers out. The Rams took advantage of four Packers' first half turnovers.

The game swung wildly towards the Packers in the second half though. Quarterback [Lynn Dickey](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Lynn_Dickey "Lynn Dickey") led the Packers to 35 unanswered points off of five touchdown drives. The Packers defense held the Rams to just four first downs in the second half, while intercepting the Rams twice and forcing a fumble. The 23-point comeback was the largest by the Packers up to that point, and was later matched in 2013 in a game against the [Dallas Cowboys](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys "Dallas Cowboys").

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

*   **Main article:**_[1981 Los Angeles Rams](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1981\_Los\_Angeles\_Rams "1981 Los Angeles Rams")_
*   **Main article:**_[1981 Green Bay Packers](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1981\_Green\_Bay\_Packers "1981 Green Bay Packers")_

[![Image 4: The side of a stadium that says Milwaukee County Stadium](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/collegefootballmania/images/3/39/06CountyStadium09-24-2000.jpg/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/180?cb=20140505172011)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/collegefootballmania/images/3/39/06CountyStadium09-24-2000.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20140505172011)

[Milwaukee County Stadium](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Milwaukee_County_Stadium "Milwaukee County Stadium") was the site of the Rams and Packers Week 1 game.

The [Los Angeles Rams](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Los_Angeles_Rams "Los Angeles Rams") and [Green Bay Packers](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers "Green Bay Packers") entered the [1982 NFL season](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_NFL_season "1982 NFL season") under vastly different circumstances. Although the Rams missed the playoffs in 1981 for the first time in eight seasons, they had been perennial contenders for most of the 1970s.[[1]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-PREDICT-1)[[2]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-2) The Packers, on the other hand, had not made the playoffs since 1972 and had not won a playoff game since 1967, under [Vince Lombardi](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Vince_Lombardi "Vince Lombardi").[[3]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-PACK-3)[Bart Starr](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Bart_Starr "Bart Starr"), who had quarterbacked the Packers during the Lombardi era, was brought in as head coach to try to revive the Packers' success of the 1960s.[[4]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-4) However, Starr accumulated a record of 39–65–2 in his first seven seasons, the worst record of any Packer coach at this point in their career.[[5]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-CHANCE1-5)[[6]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-CHANCE2-6) In 1981, the Packers went 8–8, however they missed out on the playoffs by losing the last game of the season to the [New York Jets](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/New_York_Jets "New York Jets"), 28–3.[[7]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-7) Starr signed a contract extension in the offseason based on the team's strong finish, having gone 6–2 in their last eight games.[[5]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-CHANCE1-5)[[6]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-CHANCE2-6) Going into 1982, the Packers had a strong offense, led by [Lynn Dickey](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Lynn_Dickey "Lynn Dickey"), [James Lofton](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/James_Lofton "James Lofton"), and [John Jefferson](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/John_Jefferson "John Jefferson").[[8]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-8) After missing the playoffs in 1981, the Rams brought in veteran players, signing quarterback Bert Jones and tight end Mike Barber.[[9]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-9) The Rams travelled to [Milwaukee County Stadium](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Milwaukee_County_Stadium "Milwaukee County Stadium") in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, for their Week 1 match-up against the Packers on September 12, 1982.[[1]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-PREDICT-1)

Game summary[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Famericanfootball.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2F1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### First half[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Famericanfootball.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2F1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D3&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

The Rams dominated the first half of the game, taking advantage of three Packers' turnovers to take a commanding lead into halftime. In the first quarter, Gerry Ellis fumbled the ball on a short run, which was returned by the Rams to mid-field. After a 22-yard pass from Jones to [Wendell Tyler](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Wendell_Tyler "Wendell Tyler") got the Rams close, Tyler took a short rush into the end zone to put the Rams up 7–0. Another Packers fumble, this time by Dickey while he was avoiding the Rams' pass rush, set-up another score. The Rams thought they scored a touchdown on the drive, but an offensive penalty forced them to accept a short field goal attempt, which was converted by Mike Lansford to increase the lead to 10–0. With the Packers still unable to do much on offense, the Rams scored again. After a 43-yard pass from Jones to Willie Miller put the Rams in scoring position, Jones completed an eight-yard pass to Barber for a touchdown, bringing the score to 17–0. The Rams has two more scoring drives, each ending in a Lansford field goal. The first was set-up by a long punt return, while the second came after Dickey threw an interception to Carl Ekern. The Rams took a 23–0 into halftime.[[10]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-HIGHLIGHTS-10)

### Second half[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Famericanfootball.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2F1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D4&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

The Packers returned the favor, dominating the Rams in the second half by scoring 35 unanswered points. The Packers got their first score on a short touchdown pass from Dickey to Paul Coffman. The Packers got into scoring position after a defensive pass interference penalty gave the Packers 28 yards. The Packers struck again, this time on a short run from Eddie Lee Ivery for a touchdown. The key play of the drive was a 42-yard pass completion from Dickey to Coffman. By the end of the third quarter, the Packers had cut the Rams lead to 23–14. At the beginning of the fourth quarter, the Rams were stopped by the Packers defense and attempted a long field goal, which Lansford missed. On the ensuing drive, Dickey completed a 50-yard pass to Jefferson. A few plays later, Dickey threw his second touchdown pass, a 15-yard completion to Lofton. With the score now 23–21, the Packers kicked off to the Rams. However, on the kick-off return, Robert Alexander fumbled the ball, which the Packers recovered at the 10-yard line. On the next play, Dickey threw a 10-yard touchdown pass to Coffman to give the Packers their first lead, 28–23. The Packers sealed their comeback victory with a 27-yard rushing touchdown by Ivery with about three minutes left in the game. The Packers won 35–23.[[10]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-HIGHLIGHTS-10)

### Analysis[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Famericanfootball.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2F1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D6&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

Template:Multiple image Post-game analysis focused on the comeback by the Packers and the drastic change from the first half to the second half for both teams.[[13]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-COME1-13)[[14]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-COME2-14)[[15]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-OLD1-15)[[16]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-OLD2-16) The Packers had six total turnovers, including five in the first half, while the Rams had three.[[15]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-OLD1-15)[[16]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-OLD2-16)[[11]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-PFRBOX-11) Starr considered pulling Dickey from the game at half time and putting in his back-up, although he ended up keeping him in.[[17]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-17) A fumble on a kick-off return during the fourth quarter allowed the Packers to score 14 points in under a minute of game clock.[[18]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-18) Even though the Packers lost the turnover battle, they otherwise played clean football and avoided penalties (two penalties for 15 yards); the Rams, however, had 11 penalties for 88 yards.[[11]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-PFRBOX-11) The Packers' defense was also able to stop the Rams' running game, especially in the second half.[[19]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-DEBUT-19) The Packers offense also exploded in the second half, leading to solid performances across the board for their offense skill players. Dickey threw three touchdowns, two to Coffman and one to Lofton, with Jefferson leading all receivers with six catches and 116 yards receiving yards.[[11]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-PFRBOX-11) Ivery rushed for 109 yards and two touchdowns after Ellis left the game due to an injury.[[20]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-IVERY1-20)[[21]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-IVERY2-21) Even though they gave up 23 points in the first half, the Packers defense was able to force three field goals during this period, helping to keep the game within reach.[[11]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-PFRBOX-11) The defense tightened down in the second half, only giving up four first downs to the Rams, forcing three turnovers, and shutting them out.[[19]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-DEBUT-19)[[11]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-PFRBOX-11) In total, the Packers outgained the Rams in yardage and first downs, while scoring 35 unanswered points.[[11]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-PFRBOX-11)

Aftermath[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Famericanfootball.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2F1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D7&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

The Packers continued their success, beating the [New York Giants](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/New_York_Giants "New York Giants") 27–19 the next week to start the season 2–0.[[22]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-82GNB-22) The Rams, however, lost 19–14 to the [Detroit Lions](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Detroit_Lions "Detroit Lions") in Week 2 to start the season winless.[[23]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-82RAMS-23) On September 21, 1982, the [NFL Players Association went on strike](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/National_Football_League_Players_Association#1982_strike "National Football League Players Association"). The strike originated from the players demanding a greater share of revenue, although in the end the players settled for modest increases in salary and benefits.[[24]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-FORGOT-25) As a result, the season was shortened to nine games and the playoffs were expanded to the top eight teams from each conference, regardless of division.[[25]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-FORGOT-25) The Packers ended the season 5–3–1, making the playoffs for the first time since 1972.[[22]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-82GNB-22)[[3]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-PACK-3) The Rams went 2–7 and missed out on a playoff berth.[[23]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-82RAMS-23) The [Packers beat the Arizona Cardinals 41–16](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982%E2%80%9383_NFL_playoffs#NFC:_Green_Bay_Packers_41,_St._Louis_Cardinals_16 "1982–83 NFL playoffs") in the first round of the playoffs, their first postseason victory since 1967.[[26]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-26) The Packers lost in the second round of the playoffs to the [Dallas Cowboys by a score of 37–26](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982%E2%80%9383_NFL_playoffs#NFC:_Dallas_Cowboys_37,_Green_Bay_Packers_26 "1982–83 NFL playoffs").[[27]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-27) The Rams fired head coach [Ray Malavasi](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Ray_Malavasi "Ray Malavasi") at the end of the season.[[28]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-28)

### Legacy[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Famericanfootball.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2F1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D8&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

The game marked the largest comeback in Packers' history at the time, besting the 18-point comeback during a 1965 regular season game against the Lions.[[29]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-30) This mark was matched 31 years later, with the Packers beating the [Dallas Cowboys](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys "Dallas Cowboys") during a 2013 regular season game after falling behind by 23 points; multiple post-game articles referenced the Packers matching their comeback record from the Rams game.[[31]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-32) In a 2004 article, former Packers' team historian identified the comeback as a key moment in the history of the Packers history against the Rams.[[33]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-33) Two years later, in preparation for a Packers game against the Rams, Remmel provided an in-depth overview of the comeback as part of his historical coverage. In describing the game, Remmel noted the drastic change at halftime, with the Packers defense shutting the Rams out, while Dickey and the Packers offense exploded for five touchdowns.[[34]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-34) In his book chronicling the first 100 years of Packers history, Cliff Christl described the comeback against the Rams as "an inspiring and record-setting comeback" while highlighting the contributions of Dickey, Coffman, Jefferson, and Lofton.Template:Sfn Multiple football bloggers have also written extensively about the game.[[35]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://americanfootball.fandom.com/wiki/1982_Los_Angeles_Rams_vs_Green_Bay_Packers#cite_note-36)

NFL lockout
-----------

The **NFL lockout** may refer to any of the lockouts or strikes in the history of the [National Football League](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League"):

*   The **1968 NFL strike/lockout**, which lasted 12 days before the [1968 season](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/1968_NFL_season "1968 NFL season") start.
*   The **1974 NFL strike**, which lasted for two months before the [1974 season](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/1974_NFL_season "1974 NFL season") start.
*   The **[1982 NFL strike](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/1982_NFL_strike "1982 NFL strike")**, which lasted for three months and eight weeks, forced the [1982 season](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/1982_NFL_season "1982 NFL season") to be shortened to 9 games per team.
*   The **[1987 NFL strike](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/1987_NFL_strike "1987 NFL strike")**, which lasted for 24 days and forced the [1987 season](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/1987_NFL_season "1987 NFL season") to be shortened to 15 games per team.
*   The **[2011 NFL lockout](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/2011_NFL_lockout "2011 NFL lockout")**, which lasted for over five months, resulted in cancellation of [Pro Football Hall of Fame Game](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/Pro_Football_Hall_of_Fame_Game "Pro Football Hall of Fame Game") between the [Chicago Bears](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/Chicago_Bears "Chicago Bears") and [St. Louis Rams](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/St._Louis_Rams "St. Louis Rams"), but preserves the [2011 regular season](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/2011_NFL_season "2011 NFL season").
*   The **2012 NFL referee lockout**, which lasted four months and an agreement was reached to end the lockout after increasing criticism of the NFL and the performance of the [replacement officials](https://americanfootballdatabase.fandom.com/wiki/List_of_2012_NFL_replacement_officials "List of 2012 NFL replacement officials").

See also[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Famericanfootballdatabase.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FNFL_lockout%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
